title: Argument and Informative Essays
bigQuestion: How do you turn an opinion into an essay that a careful reader has to take seriously?

story.title: Five Tries at One Sentence
story.kicker: A teacher writes a thesis on the board, erases it, and writes it again until it finally says something worth arguing.
paragraphs: Ms. Alvarez wrote one sentence on the board and stepped back. "Cell phones are a big topic in schools today." She asked the class what the sentence argued. Nobody answered, because it did not argue anything. It was true, and it was empty. You could not disagree with it, so you could not write an essay about it. She erased it.

Try two: "Cell phones are bad." Now at least someone could disagree. But a boy in the back row asked, bad for what? Bad for whom? Bad how? The sentence was a shrug with a period. She erased it. Try three: "Schools should ban cell phones because they are distracting." Better. It took a side and gave a reason. But the class had read three articles that week, and two of them said phones could help students look things up. The thesis ignored what the class actually knew.

Try four: "Schools should limit cell phone use during class because phones pull attention away from learning, even when students believe they are multitasking." Now the room got quiet in a different way. That sentence made a promise. It said what the essay would prove, and it hinted at the evidence, the studies about multitasking. Someone could argue against it. Someone would have to work to argue against it.

Try five was almost the same, with one change. Ms. Alvarez replaced "limit" with "require students to store," because "limit" was vague and the essay needed a clear policy to defend. Then she put the chalk down. Five tries, one sentence, twenty minutes. "This is the job," she said. "Not the five paragraphs. This. If the sentence argues, the essay can argue. If it does not, nothing you stack under it will help."

That is what this chapter is about: a thesis that argues, paragraphs built to support it, evidence that is explained instead of dropped, a voice that sounds like it means business, and the messy, honest process of rewriting until it works. You will also learn the shapes of informative essays, which explain rather than argue, and how to do all of this when the clock is running.
story.think: Think of an opinion you hold strongly. Could you write it as one sentence that someone else could argue against? What would they say?

lessons.title: A Claim You Can Argue
lessons.mainIdea: A thesis is one sentence that takes a position a reasonable person could disagree with, and the whole essay exists to support it.
reading: Read these two sentences. One: Chicago has many parks. Two: Chicago should turn more of its vacant lots into small neighborhood parks. The first is a fact. Nobody will argue with it, so there is nothing for an essay to do. The second is a *claim*. Someone could say no, the city should sell those lots to builders instead. That disagreement is what gives an argument essay a job.

A *thesis* is the main claim of an essay, usually stated in one sentence near the end of the introduction. A good thesis does three things. It takes a side. It is specific enough to be proved or disproved. And it is *debatable*, which means a thoughtful reader could push back. If nobody could push back, you have a topic or a fact, not a thesis.

Here is a quick test. Put the words "I believe that" in front of your sentence and then imagine someone answering, "I disagree, because..." If you can hear a real answer, you have a thesis. "I believe that Chicago has many parks." "I disagree, because..." Nothing comes. "I believe that Chicago should turn vacant lots into parks." "I disagree, because the city needs the money from selling them." That is a thesis.

One more thing. A thesis is not a question and not an announcement. "Should the school day start later?" asks; it does not claim. "This essay will discuss school start times" announces; it does not claim. "The school day should start an hour later because teenagers' bodies are wired to sleep late" claims. Write that kind of sentence.

words.d: a statement that takes a position and can be supported or challenged with reasons
the main claim of an essay, stated in one sentence, that the rest of the essay supports
open to disagreement; a thoughtful person could argue the other side

look.title: Three Sentences on the Board
look.text: A. Homework is something most students have. B. Should schools give less homework? C. Middle schools should cap homework at thirty minutes a night because more than that cuts into sleep without raising grades.
look.prompt: Which sentence is a thesis? What is wrong with each of the other two? Rewrite B so that it claims instead of asks.

check.q: Which sentence is a debatable thesis?
choices: The city should require bike lanes on every new road because they cut down on crashes.
This essay is about bike lanes.
Are bike lanes a good idea?
check.why: Only the first sentence takes a side that a reader could argue against. The others state a fact, announce a topic, or ask a question.

check.q: Why is 'Chicago has many parks' a weak thesis?
choices: Nobody could disagree with it, so there is nothing to argue
check.why: A thesis must be debatable. A plain fact gives the essay no position to defend.

check.q: What does the 'I believe that... I disagree, because...' test check?
choices: Whether the sentence is spelled correctly
Whether a reader could push back with a real reason
Whether the sentence is long enough
Whether the sentence uses first person
check.why: If you can imagine a real counterargument, the sentence is debatable, which is what a thesis needs to be.

lessons.title: Making a Thesis Specific
lessons.mainIdea: A strong thesis names a precise position and hints at the reasons, so the reader knows exactly what the essay promises to prove.
reading: "Social media is bad for teenagers." It takes a side. It is debatable. And it is still a weak thesis, because it is *vague*. Bad how? Which teenagers? Which parts of social media? The writer of that sentence has not decided what the essay will actually prove, so the essay will wander.

Compare: "Late-night scrolling harms teenagers mainly by cutting into sleep, and schools should teach students to set phone curfews." Now the reader knows the problem (lost sleep), the cause (late-night scrolling), and the position (schools should teach phone curfews). The sentence is longer, but every extra word narrows the promise. That is what *specific* means: the reader can picture what the body paragraphs will contain.

A useful shape for a first draft is claim plus because. "X should happen because A and B." The "because" part previews your reasons, which will become your body paragraphs. You do not have to keep that exact shape in the final draft, but it forces you to decide on your reasons before you start writing. Many weak essays are weak because the writer never made that decision.

Ms. Alvarez rewrote her thesis five times. Each version got narrower. That is normal. Expect your first thesis to be a rough guess at what you think. Write the essay, find out what you can actually prove, and then go back and rewrite the thesis to match. The final thesis is often the last sentence you fix.

words.d: not clear or specific; leaving the reader unsure what is meant
precise and detailed enough that the reader can picture exactly what is claimed
to give the reader a short look ahead at what is coming

look.title: Five Versions of a Thesis
look.text: 1. School lunch is a topic. 2. School lunch is bad. 3. School lunch should be better. 4. Our school should serve more fresh food at lunch. 5. Our school should replace two fried items a week with fresh fruit and vegetables, because students who eat better in the afternoon focus better in class.
look.prompt: What does each version add that the one before it lacked? Which words in version 5 tell you what the body paragraphs will be about?

check.q: What is the main problem with 'Social media is bad for teenagers' as a thesis?
choices: It is written in first person
It is too vague to tell the reader what the essay will prove
check.why: The sentence takes a side, but 'bad' and 'social media' are so broad that the essay could go anywhere.

check.q: What does the 'because' part of a claim-plus-because thesis do?
choices: It previews the reasons that will become body paragraphs
It makes the sentence sound formal
It replaces the need for evidence
It tells the reader the essay's length
check.why: The reasons after 'because' map out the body of the essay and force the writer to decide on them early.

check.q: When is it normal to rewrite your thesis?
choices: Never; the first version must stand
After drafting, once you know what you can actually prove
check.why: Writers often discover their real argument while drafting, then go back and sharpen the thesis to match.

lessons.title: The Introduction
lessons.mainIdea: An introduction earns the reader's attention, gives the background they need, and ends with the thesis.
reading: Read this opening. "On a Tuesday in March, a seventh grader in Rockford fell asleep in second period for the third time that week. She was not lazy. She had been awake until one in the morning, and school started at 7:30." Then, two sentences later: "Middle schools should start no earlier than 8:30, because teenagers' sleep cycles shift later and early starts cost them learning." That is an *introduction* doing its three jobs in order.

Job one is the *hook*, the first sentence or two that makes a reader want the next one. A hook can be a brief scene, a surprising fact, a sharp question, or a short quotation. It should connect to your argument, not just grab attention. A hook about sharks in an essay about sleep is a trick, and readers do not like tricks.

Job two is *background*: the few facts a reader needs before the thesis will make sense. For the sleep essay, that might be what time local schools start and what doctors say about teenage sleep. Keep it short. Two or three sentences usually do it. The body paragraphs will carry the detail.

Job three is the thesis, and in most school essays it comes last in the introduction. That placement is not a rule of nature, but it works: the reader arrives at your claim with the background already in hand, and the body paragraphs can begin immediately. Hook, background, thesis. Learn the order, and later you can bend it.

words.d: the opening paragraph of an essay, which hooks the reader, gives background, and states the thesis
the first sentence or two, written to make the reader want to keep reading
the basic facts a reader needs before the thesis will make sense

look.title: Four Hooks for One Essay
look.text: An essay argues that the school should add a second lunch period. Hook A: "Lunch is an important part of the day." Hook B: "At 11:52 the line is forty students long, and the bell rings at 12:15." Hook C: "Have you ever wondered about lunch?" Hook D: "Sharks can smell blood from far away."
look.prompt: Rank the four hooks from best to worst and explain each ranking. What does the best one do that the others do not?

check.q: In what order do the three parts of a standard introduction usually appear?
check.why: The hook draws the reader in, background prepares them, and the thesis lands last so the body can begin.

check.q: Why is a hook about sharks a bad choice for an essay about school start times?
choices: It does not connect to the argument, so it feels like a trick
check.why: A hook must lead toward the thesis. Attention grabbed for no reason is wasted and annoys the reader.

check.q: How much background should an introduction give?
choices: All the evidence for the thesis
None; save everything for the body
Only the few facts needed for the thesis to make sense
check.why: Background is brief. Detail belongs in the body paragraphs.

lessons.title: Body Paragraphs and Topic Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: Each body paragraph makes one point that supports the thesis, states it in a topic sentence, and then proves it.
reading: Look at the first sentence of a body paragraph from the sleep essay: "Early start times hurt learning because tired students remember less of what they hear." That sentence is a *topic sentence*. It states the single point of the paragraph, and it clearly connects to the thesis. A reader who saw only the topic sentences of an essay should be able to follow the whole argument.

A *body paragraph* is the essay's working unit. Each one has a job: prove one reason from your thesis. Inside it, a simple pattern holds up well. Topic sentence. Evidence, such as a fact, a study, an example, or a quotation. Explanation of how that evidence proves the point. Sometimes a second piece of evidence and a second explanation. Then a sentence that closes the point or leads to the next paragraph.

The most common problem is a paragraph that tries to do two jobs. "Early starts hurt learning, and also buses would run better later." Those are two reasons, so they need two paragraphs. When you find an "and also" in a topic sentence, split it. A second common problem is a topic sentence that is just a fact: "Many schools start at 7:30." A fact does not argue. Make the sentence claim something.

Order matters too. Put your strongest reason either first or last, where readers pay the most attention. A middle paragraph can carry a weaker reason. And use *transitions* between paragraphs, words or phrases like "in addition," "more important," or "even so," so the reader knows how each new point relates to the last one.

words.d: a middle paragraph of an essay that proves one reason supporting the thesis
the sentence, usually first, that states the single point a paragraph will prove
a word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next, such as 'in addition' or 'however'

look.title: One Paragraph, Labeled
look.text: Early start times hurt learning because tired students remember less. (topic) In one study, students who slept less than seven hours scored lower on a memory test the next morning. (evidence) That gap shows up in class as forgotten instructions and repeated lessons. (explanation) A later bell would give those students the sleep their memory depends on. (close)
look.prompt: Cover the labels. Can you still tell which sentence does which job? What would be lost if the explanation sentence were cut?

check.q: What should a topic sentence do?
choices: State the single point the paragraph will prove
Restate the thesis word for word
Introduce a new topic unrelated to the thesis
check.why: A topic sentence names the paragraph's one point and ties it to the thesis.

check.q: A topic sentence reads: 'Uniforms save families money, and also they reduce bullying.' What is the problem?
choices: It contains two reasons that need two paragraphs
check.why: Each body paragraph should prove one point. Two reasons in one topic sentence means the paragraph will split its attention.

check.q: Where should your strongest reason usually go?
choices: First or last, where readers pay the most attention
check.why: Readers attend most to what comes first and last, so those positions carry the strongest points.

lessons.title: The Conclusion
lessons.mainIdea: A conclusion restates the argument in fresh words and shows the reader why it matters beyond the essay.
reading: Here is a weak conclusion: "In conclusion, schools should start later because of sleep and learning. Thank you for reading." It repeats the thesis with fewer words and then apologizes for existing. Readers can feel the writer running for the exit. A *conclusion* should feel like the writer stopped on purpose.

A conclusion has two jobs. First, remind the reader of the argument, but in new words and with the weight of the evidence behind it. You are not introducing the claim now; you are confirming it. "By 8:30 a seventh grader is awake, fed and able to hold a lesson in her head. By 7:30 she is not. The bell should follow the body." Same claim, different sentences, more confidence.

Second, answer the question so what. Why should the reader care now that the essay is over? You might name what happens if nothing changes, suggest one concrete next step, or connect the argument to something larger. "A later bell will not fix every problem in a middle school. But it fixes one, for every student, every morning." That is a *closing thought*, and it is where the reader decides whether the essay was worth it.

Avoid three habits. Do not add a brand-new reason; if it was important, it needed a body paragraph. Do not begin with "In conclusion"; the reader knows where they are. And do not end with a question you never answered. A conclusion is a landing, not a takeoff.

words.d: the final paragraph of an essay, which confirms the argument and shows why it matters
the last idea in a conclusion, which answers 'so what' and gives the reader a reason to care

look.title: Two Endings
look.text: Ending A: "In conclusion, the city should add more bus routes for the reasons I said. That is my opinion." Ending B: "A bus that comes every ten minutes changes what a neighborhood can be. It decides whether a nurse makes her shift and whether a student makes first period. The city can keep printing maps of routes that do not exist, or it can send the buses."
look.prompt: What does Ending B do that Ending A does not? Point to the sentence that answers 'so what.' Then rewrite Ending A in your own fresh words.

check.q: What are the two jobs of a conclusion?
choices: Add a new reason and ask a question
Restate the hook and list all evidence
Confirm the argument in fresh words and show why it matters
check.why: A conclusion reminds the reader of the claim with new wording and then answers 'so what.'

check.q: Why should a conclusion not introduce a new reason?
choices: Reasons belong in body paragraphs, where they can be proved
Readers stop reading at the last paragraph
check.why: A reason dropped in at the end has no evidence or explanation behind it and weakens the essay.

check.q: Which sentence is a closing thought that answers 'so what'?
choices: In conclusion, I have shown my three reasons.
A later bell fixes one problem for every student, every morning.
check.why: That sentence tells the reader why the argument matters now. The others repeat, ask, or state a bare fact.

lessons.title: Bringing in Evidence and Quotations
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence must be introduced, quoted or summarized accurately, and credited, so the reader knows where it came from and why it is there.
reading: Read this: "Students need sleep. 'Teenagers need eight to ten hours a night.' So schools should start later." The quotation in the middle appears from nowhere. Who said it? Why should we trust them? It is a *dropped quotation*, and readers stumble over it. Now read: "According to the pediatrician who wrote the school's health guide, 'Teenagers need eight to ten hours a night.'" Same words, but now the reader knows the source and can weigh it.

There are three ways to bring *evidence* into an essay. You can quote, using the exact words inside quotation marks. You can *paraphrase*, restating the idea in your own words at about the same length. Or you can summarize, boiling a long passage down to its main point. Quote when the exact wording matters. Paraphrase or summarize when only the idea matters. Most essays should use far more paraphrase than quotation.

Whichever you choose, do three things. Introduce the source with a *signal phrase* such as "According to," "The report found," or "As Douglass writes." Report it accurately; changing a quotation's words or a study's numbers is a kind of lying. And credit it, so the reader can find it. In a school essay, that means naming the author or source in the sentence or in parentheses after it.

Length matters. A quotation should be as short as it can be while still making the point. If you find yourself quoting three sentences, ask which phrase actually matters and quote only that. Frederick Douglass, in his 1845 autobiography, wrote the line "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man." You would quote that exact sentence, because its shape is the point. You would paraphrase the paragraph around it.

words.d: facts, examples, data, or quotations used to support a claim
to restate a source's idea in your own words, at about the same length
words that introduce a source, such as 'According to the report' or 'As the author notes'
a quotation placed in an essay with no introduction, so the reader does not know its source or purpose

look.title: A Sentence Worth Quoting
look.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
look.cite: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
look.prompt: Why would a writer quote this sentence instead of paraphrasing it? Write a signal phrase that could introduce it in an essay.

check.q: What is a dropped quotation?
choices: A quotation that is too long
A quotation with a misspelled word
A quotation placed in the essay with no introduction or source
check.why: A dropped quotation appears without a signal phrase or credit, so the reader cannot tell where it came from or why it is there.

check.q: When should you quote instead of paraphrase?
choices: When the source's exact wording matters
When the source is very long
check.why: Quote when the precise words carry the point. Otherwise, paraphrase or summarize in your own words.

check.q: Which of these is a signal phrase?
check.why: A signal phrase introduces a source and tells the reader who is speaking.

lessons.title: Explaining Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence does not speak for itself; after every piece of evidence, the writer must explain how it proves the point.
reading: A student writes: "Schools should start later. A study found that students at a school that moved its start time to 8:30 had fewer car crashes." Then the paragraph ends. The evidence is good. But the student has left the reader to do the thinking. What do car crashes have to do with learning? Why did the crashes drop? The paragraph is a sandwich with no filling.

*Reasoning* is the sentence or two that follows evidence and connects it to the claim. It answers the question, "So what does this prove?" For the crash study: "Fewer crashes means the students were more alert, and an alert student behind the wheel at 7:45 is also an alert student in a classroom at 8:00. The same sleep that prevents a crash lets a lesson stick." Now the evidence is doing work for the argument.

A useful habit is to follow every piece of evidence with the phrase "This shows that" in your draft, and then finish the sentence. Later you can cut the phrase itself. If you cannot finish the sentence, the evidence does not fit your point, and you should find better evidence or change the point. Claim, evidence, reasoning: that three-part rhythm is the skeleton of every good body paragraph.

Reasoning is also where you deal with the other side. Naming a *counterargument*, the strongest objection to your claim, and answering it fairly, makes a reader trust you. "Some argue that a later start would push after-school jobs and sports later too. That is true, and it is a real cost. But an hour of lost practice time does not compare to a year of lessons half-heard." That is not weakness. That is confidence.

words.d: the explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it
the strongest objection to your claim, which a careful writer names and answers

look.title: Finish the Sentence
look.text: Claim: The school should plant trees along the front parking lot. Evidence: In a survey, 62 percent of students said the lot is the hottest place on campus in May and September. This shows that...
look.prompt: Finish the reasoning sentence so the evidence proves the claim. Then write one counterargument and a fair answer to it.

check.q: What does reasoning do in a body paragraph?
choices: Explains how the evidence proves the claim
Introduces the source of a quotation
check.why: Reasoning is the link between evidence and claim. Without it, the reader has to guess why the evidence is there.

check.q: If you cannot finish 'This shows that...' after a piece of evidence, what should you do?
choices: Quote the evidence a second time
Find evidence that fits, or change the point
check.why: Evidence that cannot be connected to the claim is not supporting it. Either the evidence or the point must change.

check.q: Why does answering a counterargument make an essay stronger?
choices: It shows the writer has considered the other side and can still defend the claim
It proves the other side is dishonest
check.why: Readers trust a writer who names the best objection and answers it fairly.

lessons.title: Formal Style and Objective Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Argument and informative essays use a formal style and an objective tone so the reader focuses on the evidence, not the writer's feelings.
reading: Two sentences, same idea. One: "Honestly the cafeteria food is so gross, everybody hates it, I mean come on." Two: "In a school survey, 71 percent of students rated the cafeteria food below average." The first sounds like a text message. The second sounds like someone worth listening to. The difference is not intelligence. It is *style* and *tone*.

A *formal style* means the language of writing rather than the language of hallway talk. Use complete sentences. Avoid slang and contractions like "gonna" or "can't" in a final draft. Choose precise words: not "a lot of kids," but "most seventh graders" or "seventy percent of students." Do not write "I think" or "in my opinion" before every claim; the essay is your opinion, so just state the claim.

An *objective tone* means you sound fair, even when you are arguing hard. Objective does not mean without a position. It means your position rests on evidence rather than on how loudly you feel. Words like "gross," "stupid," "obviously" and "everybody knows" tell the reader you are upset; they do not tell the reader you are right. Cut them and let the numbers, examples and reasoning carry the weight.

Formal does not mean stiff or fancy. "The aforementioned nutritional deficiencies necessitate reform" is formal and terrible. "The lunch menu needs to change, and the survey shows why" is formal and clear. Aim for the voice of a calm expert explaining something to a smart stranger. That voice is not something you are born with. It is something you practice.

words.d: writing that uses complete sentences, precise words and no slang, suited to essays and reports
a fair, even voice that rests on evidence rather than on the writer's feelings
the writer's attitude toward the subject, as heard in word choice and sentence style

look.title: Same Paragraph, Two Voices
look.text: Version A: Our library is basically dead. Nobody goes, it's boring, and the books are ancient. Version B: The library's checkout records show a 40 percent drop in loans over three years, and more than half of its collection was published before 2000. The problem is not that students dislike reading; it is that the shelves offer little they want to read.
look.prompt: List every word in Version A that signals feeling rather than evidence. What does Version B use instead? Which version would a principal act on?

check.q: Which sentence has an objective tone?
choices: The new schedule is obviously a disaster and everyone hates it.
Honestly, the schedule is the worst thing ever.
Under the new schedule, average tardies rose from 12 to 31 a day.
I think the schedule is kind of bad, I guess.
check.why: That sentence reports evidence in a fair, even voice. The others rely on feeling words or hedging.

check.q: Why should you cut 'I think' from before most claims in an essay?
choices: The essay is already your opinion, so the phrase adds nothing
First person is illegal in writing
It makes the sentence too long
check.why: Readers know the claims are yours. Stating them directly sounds more confident.

check.q: What does 'formal' NOT mean?
check.why: Formal style is clear and precise. Stuffing sentences with big words makes writing worse, not more formal.

lessons.title: Compare, Contrast, Cause and Effect
lessons.mainIdea: Informative essays explain rather than argue, and two of their most useful shapes are compare-and-contrast and cause-and-effect.
reading: Not every essay argues. An *informative essay* explains something the reader wants to understand: how a process works, how two things differ, why something happened. It still needs a controlling idea in one sentence, but that sentence promises understanding rather than a fight. "Chicago's two baseball parks reflect two different ideas about what a ballpark is for" is informative. It sets up an explanation, not a debate.

The *compare-and-contrast* essay explains two subjects by their likenesses and differences. It has two common shapes. In the block shape, you cover everything about subject A, then everything about subject B. In the point-by-point shape, you take one feature at a time: age of the park, then neighborhood, then seating, and cover both subjects under each. Point-by-point is usually clearer for readers, because they never have to hold subject A in memory while reading about B.

The *cause-and-effect* essay explains why something happens or what follows from it. The 1871 Chicago fire is a classic subject. Causes: a long dry summer, a city built mostly of wood, a strong wind from the southwest. Effects: about a third of the city destroyed, new building codes, and a rebuilt downtown that became a laboratory for tall buildings. The essay can move from causes to the event, or from the event to its effects, or both.

Two warnings. First, do not confuse before with because. The fire came after a dry summer, and the dry summer helped cause it; but not everything that comes before something causes it. Second, in compare-and-contrast, do not just list. "A is old; B is new. A is north; B is south." A list is not an explanation. Tell the reader what the differences add up to. That is the controlling idea doing its job.

words.d: an essay that explains a subject clearly rather than arguing a position
an essay shape that explains two subjects through their similarities and differences
an essay shape that explains why something happens or what results from it

look.title: Two Outlines for the Same Essay
look.text: Block: Paragraph 2, all about walking to school. Paragraph 3, all about taking the bus. Point-by-point: Paragraph 2, time (walking vs. bus). Paragraph 3, cost (walking vs. bus). Paragraph 4, what you notice along the way (walking vs. bus).
look.prompt: Which outline makes it easier for a reader to compare the two? When might the block shape be the better choice?

check.q: How does an informative essay differ from an argument essay?
choices: It explains a subject rather than defending a debatable claim
check.why: Informative writing aims at understanding; argument aims at persuasion. Both use evidence and a controlling idea.

check.q: In a point-by-point compare-and-contrast essay, how are paragraphs organized?
choices: All of subject A, then all of subject B
One feature at a time, covering both subjects under each
check.why: Point-by-point takes each feature in turn and compares both subjects under it, so readers never lose track.

check.q: 'The fire happened after the summer, so the summer caused the fire.' What mistake is this?
check.why: Coming before something is not the same as causing it. A cause-and-effect essay must show the actual link.

lessons.title: Defining a Term
lessons.mainIdea: A definition essay explains what a word or idea really means by placing it in a class, separating it from its neighbors, and showing examples.
reading: What is courage? A dictionary gives you a line. A *definition essay* gives you the idea itself: what it includes, what it does not, and what it looks like in a real life. Writers choose this form for words people use loosely, such as courage, friendship, fairness, or home. The essay's controlling idea is the writer's own careful definition.

A strong definition has three moves. First, put the term in a *class*: courage is a kind of choice. Second, tell what separates it from other members of that class: it is a choice made while afraid, not one made without fear. Third, give *examples* and non-examples. A student who reads her poem aloud with her hands shaking shows courage. A student who is not scared of anything and jumps off a diving board does not, at least not by this definition; that is boldness, or maybe just fun.

The examples are where the essay comes alive. Abstract words stay abstract until a reader sees a person doing something. Choose two or three examples that show different sides of the term: courage in a hospital, courage in a friendship, courage in front of a class. Each example becomes a body paragraph, with its own topic sentence explaining which part of the definition it shows.

One trap to avoid: do not open with "The dictionary defines courage as..." Readers have seen that opening a thousand times, and it hands your job to someone else. Start with a scene, a question, or a case that does not quite fit the usual meaning. Then earn your own definition across the essay.

words.d: an informative essay that explains the full meaning of a term through class, distinctions and examples
the larger group a thing belongs to, such as 'a kind of choice' or 'a type of feeling'
a specific case that shows what a general idea looks like in real life

look.title: A Definition in Three Moves
look.text: A friend is not simply someone you like. A friend is a person (class) who tells you the truth when a stranger would stay polite (what sets it apart). When Marcus told me my speech was boring the night before the contest, I was angry for an hour and grateful for a year (example).
look.prompt: Find the class, the distinction and the example. Then write the same three moves for the word 'home.'

check.q: What are the three moves of a strong definition?
choices: Class, what sets it apart, examples
check.why: A definition places the term in a group, separates it from its neighbors, and shows it in action.

check.q: Why should a definition essay include non-examples?
choices: They show where the definition's edge is, which sharpens it
Every essay must have exactly two of them
They replace the need for examples
check.why: Showing what does not count for the term clarifies what does.

check.q: Why is 'The dictionary defines courage as...' a weak opening?
choices: It hands the writer's job to someone else and readers have seen it too often
check.why: The essay's purpose is the writer's own definition. Borrowing the dictionary's line at the start gives that up.

lessons.title: Real Revision
lessons.mainIdea: Revision means re-seeing the whole essay and changing what it says and how it is built, not just fixing commas.
reading: A student finishes a draft, runs spell check, changes two commas, and calls it revised. That is *editing*, and it matters, but it is the last step, not the main one. *Revision* means literally to see again. It asks bigger questions. Does the thesis still match what the essay proves? Is any body paragraph doing two jobs? Is there evidence with no reasoning after it? Would the essay be stronger if paragraph four came second?

The *writing process* is usually described in stages: plan, draft, revise, edit, publish. Real writers loop through those stages more than once. Ms. Alvarez rewrote her thesis five times before the class had drafted anything; that was revision happening during planning. You might draft a body paragraph, realize your thesis is wrong, and go back. That is not failure. That is the process working.

Here is a revision routine that catches the big problems. Read the essay aloud; your ear will catch what your eye skips. Then write each topic sentence on a separate line and read only those. If the list does not make an argument, the essay does not either. Then find every quotation or statistic and check that a sentence of reasoning follows it. Then, and only then, fix the commas.

Real revision often means cutting. A paragraph you liked may not fit the thesis you ended up with. Cut it and save it somewhere; it may fit another essay. Writers who cannot cut end up with essays that are long and weak. Writers who can cut end up with essays that are short and strong. Nobody ever complained that an argument was too clear.

words.d: re-seeing a draft and changing its ideas, structure and evidence, not just its surface
fixing spelling, punctuation, grammar and word choice after the ideas are settled
the stages of planning, drafting, revising, editing and publishing, which writers loop through

look.title: One Essay, Three Drafts
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a model essay written for this chapter
look.prompt: The essay got shorter while its evidence more than doubled. What must the writer have cut? Why might that make the essay stronger?

check.q: Which of these is revision rather than editing?
choices: Moving a body paragraph so the strongest reason comes first
check.why: Revision changes structure and ideas. The other choices are surface fixes, which is editing.

check.q: Why read only the topic sentences during revision?
choices: It saves time so you can skip the rest
Topic sentences are the only part graded
If they do not make an argument together, the essay does not either
check.why: The topic sentences are the skeleton of the argument. Reading them alone reveals gaps and repeats.

check.q: What does it mean that the writing process 'loops'?
choices: Each essay must be written twice
Writers move backward to earlier stages when they discover a problem
The stages happen in one fixed order
check.why: Real writers go back to planning or drafting when revision shows the thesis or structure is wrong.

lessons.title: Writing Under a Time Limit
lessons.mainIdea: When the clock is running, spend the first minutes planning a thesis and three reasons, and save the last minutes to check what you wrote.
reading: The prompt appears, the timer starts, and a student begins writing the first sentence that comes to mind. Twenty minutes later she has a page and a half that argues two different things. Writing *on demand*, as on a test or a timed class assignment, rewards planning more than any other kind of writing, because there is no second draft. The plan is the draft.

Use a rough budget. In a forty-minute essay, spend the first five minutes reading the *prompt* twice, underlining what it actually asks, and writing a thesis and three reasons on scratch paper. Spend thirty minutes drafting, one paragraph per reason, with one piece of evidence and one sentence of reasoning in each. Spend the last five minutes reading what you wrote and fixing anything unclear. Students who skip the first five minutes almost always lose more than five minutes wandering.

Read the prompt like a contract. If it says "argue," take a side. If it says "explain," do not. If it says "use evidence from the passage," quote or paraphrase the passage, and name where the evidence came from. Many low scores come from good writing that answered a different question. Underline the verb in the prompt and check your thesis against it before you write anything else.

When time runs short, protect the shape. A finished essay with three short body paragraphs beats an unfinished one with two long ones. If you have two minutes left and no conclusion, write two sentences: restate the claim in new words, and say why it matters. Then stop. Readers forgive a plain ending. They do not forgive a missing one.

words.d: writing done in one sitting under a time limit, such as on a test
the question or task that tells the writer what to write about and how
a plan for how to divide limited time among planning, drafting and checking

look.title: A Forty-Minute Budget
look.cite: a suggested plan written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which part of this budget do most students skip? What goes wrong when they do? How would you adjust it for a twenty-minute essay?

check.q: What should you do in the first five minutes of a timed essay?
choices: Write the introduction as fast as possible
Read the prompt twice, then write a thesis and three reasons
Skip planning and start the body
check.why: Planning a thesis and reasons prevents the essay from wandering, and there is no second draft to fix it later.

check.q: Why underline the verb in a prompt?
choices: Underlining is required for full credit
It shows you what the prompt actually asks: argue, explain, compare
It counts toward the word limit
check.why: The verb tells you the kind of essay. Answering a different question than the one asked costs points.

check.q: With two minutes left and no conclusion, what should you do?
choices: Write two sentences: restate the claim and say why it matters
check.why: A short conclusion gives the essay a finished shape. Readers forgive plain endings, not missing ones.

review.q: Which sentence would work as the thesis of an argument essay?
choices: The state should fund a free bus to state parks from Chicago because most city students never see one.
This essay will discuss state parks.
review.why: Only the second sentence takes a specific, debatable position and previews a reason.

review.q: Where does the thesis usually appear in a school essay?
choices: In the first sentence of the essay
At the end of the introduction
In the middle of a body paragraph
review.why: The hook and background come first; the thesis lands at the end of the introduction so the body can begin.

review.q: A body paragraph gives a statistic and then ends. What is missing?
choices: Reasoning that explains how the statistic proves the point
review.why: Evidence never speaks for itself. Reasoning connects it to the claim.

review.q: Which sentence uses a signal phrase to introduce evidence?
choices: As the city's transit report found, ridership fell 20 percent.
review.why: 'As the city's transit report found' tells the reader who the source is before the evidence appears.

review.q: Which word choice best fits a formal, objective tone?
choices: Everybody knows the plan won't work.
The plan's own budget shows a shortfall in year two.
review.why: That sentence relies on evidence in plain, precise language rather than on feeling words.

review.q: An essay explains how the 1871 fire led to new building codes. What is its shape?
review.why: The essay explains what resulted from an event, which is cause and effect.

review.q: Which of these is real revision rather than editing?
choices: Rewriting the thesis to match what the body actually proves
Changing a period to a semicolon
review.why: Revision changes ideas and structure. The other choices are surface edits.

review.q: In a timed essay, why does a finished essay with short paragraphs beat an unfinished one with long paragraphs?
choices: Short paragraphs are always better writing
Long paragraphs are against the rules
Timed essays are graded only on length
Readers need the whole shape, including a conclusion, to follow the argument
review.why: The complete shape carries the argument. A missing conclusion leaves the reader without a landing.
